summary: Examines how the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) can identify the user-level service that a call is being used for. It discusses why this is useful, lays out architectural principles, warns of problems when done poorly such as fraud and interoperability failures, and recommends good practices. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone call arrives, how does the system know if it's a voice call, a video chat, or something else? This explains how to tell, and what goes wrong if you guess.

questions: how to identify communication services in sip
how to identify services in sip
subtitle: How networks can determine what service a call really is, and why pretending it's something else breaks everything.

tldr.problem: When a SIP endpoint initiates a call, the network must determine what the user is actually doing with it: a voice call, a video chat, a game, media streaming, or something else. Getting this identification wrong causes fraud, incompatibility between networks, and blocks new kinds of services.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC argues that service identity should always be derived from the explicit signaling (media types, target URIs, content types, and capabilities), never from a user-provided service identifier. Derived identification ensures the service matches what actually happens on the network.
tldr.outcome: When service identification is done properly (derived from signaling), the network gains what it needs: routing to the right endpoint software, authorization checks, billing accuracy, and quality-of-service policies that actually apply to the intended service.

facts.label: Service examples discussed
facts.value: IPTV, multimedia conferencing, gaming, voice chat, messaging

today: RFC 5897 is an Informational document that has guided thinking about service identification in SIP networks. It has influenced recommendations against adding abstract service identifier fields to SIP headers, and has supported the approach of using URIs and explicit SDP signaling to distinguish between different uses of SIP.

sections.title: What Service Are We Using?
sections.content:
Service identification means figuring out what the user is actually doing with a SIP session. A SIP INVITE that carries audio could be a voice call between two phones, a push-to-talk session on a mobile, a conference call, audio content from a server, or many other things. Each has a different user experience and different network requirements.

Networks need to know the service for several practical reasons: to route a call to the right software on the user's device (a gaming app vs. a phone app), to apply the correct security policies or quality-of-service rules, to bill the user correctly, to handle how many devices can ring at once, or to decide if this user is even allowed to use this service. Getting the service wrong causes chaos: a call that should ring on a gaming device rings on a phone, or content that should be free gets charged as a premium service.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone needs to know if an incoming call is a normal phone call (so it looks like your dialer) or a gaming chat (so it opens the game instead). If the phone guesses wrong, you miss the call.

sections.title: Two Approaches: Declared vs. Derived
sections.content:
There are two fundamentally different ways to identify a service. In declarative service identification, the user agent (the calling device) explicitly puts a service identifier into the SIP message, something like a Service-ID: voice-chat header. The network trusts this field and uses it to make decisions. In derived service identification, the network reads the actual signaling (the media types in the SDP, the target URI, the message content type) and figures out what service this is from the protocol details alone.

The RFC argues strongly that derived identification is the only approach that works. Declarative identifiers give the calling user agency to announce one thing while actually doing something else. The network cannot distinguish between "this really is a multimedia conference" and "I'm claiming this is a conference but I'm actually using this for something cheaper." Derived identification, by contrast, reads what the user is actually doing and infers the service from that.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask someone what they are ordering (declarative), they might lie to get a discount. If you watch what they actually pick off the shelf (derived), they cannot lie about what they bought.

sections.title: Where Service Identification Is Used
sections.content:
Within a user agent (endpoint), service identification routes the incoming request to the right software component. If a device runs both a voice-calling app and a gaming app that both use SIP, the SIP layer must know which one should handle a particular incoming call. Without identification, a gaming message to play a move might appear on the voice-calling screen.

In the network, service identification drives application invocation: different servers for different services (a media server for IPTV, a conference server for meetings). It controls quality-of-service decisions (real-time voice needs low latency; downloaded movies do not). It enables service authorization (does this user have permission to use IPTV?) and billing (voice by the minute, movies by the item). It dispatches to the right device when a user has multiple phones. These are all valuable uses, but all of them break if the service identifier cannot be trusted.
sections.plainLanguage: The network uses service identification to decide: does this request need a fast lane or a normal lane? Should it go to the voice server or the video server? Is this person supposed to be watching TV? How much to charge?

sections.title: Why Declarative Service Identification Fails
sections.content:
Fraud: If billing is based on the service identifier in the message, a user can send signaling for an expensive service but claim it is a cheap one. A user sends an INVITE for high-definition video (expensive per-gigabyte billing) but declares it as Service-ID: audio-only (cheaper per-minute billing). The user gets the video but pays the audio rate.

Interoperability failures: Different network operators can name the same service differently or omit support for a service identifier they do not recognize. If domain A and domain B interconnect, and domain A sends Service-ID: voice-chat but domain B has never heard of that identifier, domain B cannot apply the right policies, assign the right quality of service, or know what the user is trying to do. Derived identification avoids this: both domains inspect the actual SDP and media types and derive their own understanding of the service, without needing to agree on a standardized list.

Stifling innovation: Declarative identifiers require global agreement: if service identifiers are to mean the same thing everywhere, all operators must agree on a fixed list. Once such a list exists, introducing a new service (like avatar-enhanced video conferencing) requires all existing operators to update their systems, or the new service breaks on their networks. This creates pressure for homogeneity and discourages the heterogeneity and innovation that SIP was designed to enable.
sections.plainLanguage: If you declare the service, you can lie. If you don't agree with the person checking, they may not know what you want. And if everyone has to agree on every possible service ahead of time, nobody can invent new ones.

sections.title: Core Principles of Service Identification
sections.content:
A service is a by-product of signaling. When a user sends an INVITE to a media server with audio and video SDP, the result of that action is an IPTV session. The service is not separate from the signaling; it is what happens when the signaling is processed. Therefore, derived service identification is always possible: the network can always read what the signaling is and figure out what service resulted.

Identical signaling produces identical services. If two INVITEs have the same target, same media types, same codecs, and same header fields, they must produce the same user experience. If they seem to produce different services, something is being overlooked: perhaps the target URI is actually different (a media server vs. a user), or a content type difference is not being signaled explicitly, or the signaling mechanism is incomplete and needs to be extended. The answer is never to add a separate field that claims to be a service identifier.

URIs are key. The Request-URI (the target of the INVITE) is an excellent mechanism for differentiation. When a service is not a call to a user but a call to a specific resource or software instance (a particular video service, a gaming instance), targeting it at a different URI makes this explicit and unambiguous. This is far better than trying to announce the service separately.
sections.plainLanguage: The service is what actually happens, not what you say is happening. If two messages look identical, they must produce the same thing. And if you really want something different, ask for a different thing (use a different address), don't just say it is different.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC recommends five practices. First, always derive service identity from explicit signaling: read the SDP, the target URI, the content types, and the capabilities, and infer the service from those. Never trust a service identifier field. Second, design for negotiation: SIP endpoints can negotiate media types and capabilities, and this negotiation may change what service ends up being provided. Build service logic that expects this flexibility, not a fixed list of services.

Third, use presence systems to help endpoints publish URIs for specific services, so a device can offer the URI of its gaming app, its video app, and its voice app separately, making the signaling explicit. Fourth, keep service identifiers intra-domain only: if a domain needs to cache service identity for performance, that is okay for internal operations, but never pass it to another domain. Fifth, dispatch devices based on feature tags, not abstract service identifiers—feature tags describe concrete SIP capabilities, whereas service identifiers are vague abstract labels.
sections.plainLanguage: Read what is actually being sent, not what someone claims is being sent. Let endpoints talk about what they can do, and different places can have different names for the same thing. Use real addresses to pick different services, not hidden claims.
